props.title: Sorry, Wrong Number
props.initialSlug: Bedridden woman overhears murder plot by phone

sections.content: Sorry, Wrong Number revolutionized the thriller genre by confining its protagonist to a single location while building unbearable tension. Barbara Stanwyck delivers a tour-de-force performance as Leona Stevenson, a bedridden woman who overhears a murder plot through a crossed telephone line. The film masterfully adapts Lucille Fletcher's radio play, expanding it into a complex noir that influenced countless "confined space" thrillers like Rear Window (1954) and Phone Booth (2002). Director Anatole Litvak uses innovative sound design and claustrophobic camera angles to create a suffocating atmosphere of helplessness.

sections.content: The telephone as a source of terror became a defining noir trope after Sorry, Wrong Number. Films like Black Christmas (1974) and When a Stranger Calls (1979) built entire narratives around threatening phone calls, while The Night of the Hunter (1955) used phone conversations to create narrative tension. Stanwyck's performance as the increasingly panicked Leona set a template for vulnerable-yet-resourceful protagonists that influenced characters in films like Misery (1990) and Panic Room (2002). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Single-Location Thrillers

The confined setting of Sorry, Wrong Number proved that limitation could breed innovation. The film's influence can be seen in modern single-location thrillers like Buried (2010), where Ryan Reynolds spends the entire film in a coffin, and Locke (2013), which never leaves Tom Hardy's car. These films follow Litvak's lead in using restricted space to heighten psychological tension. Even contemporary phone-centric thrillers like The Guilty (2018) and its American remake draw direct inspiration from the way Sorry, Wrong Number builds suspense through voice and sound alone.
